newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers keep up protest, cut road links.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers keep up protest, cut road links.

text.p: Thousands of protesting farmers cut Greece's main north-south road and rail links for a third day on Saturday, posing the toughest challenge to date to the socialist government.

The farmers blocked the national highway and railway near the central town of Larissa with some 5,000 tractors, cutting all main land links between Athens and Greece's second city of Salonika in the north, police said.

They said farmers had seized toll booths and barricaded the national road in five places, demanding better price supports, lower fuel costs and the rescheduling of $1.3 billion in debts owed by farm cooperatives to the state Agricultural Bank.
The farmers, flying black flags on their tractors, branched out through sideroads between Larissa and Salonika to stop trucks and buses from skirting the main highway, police said.
Government officials said they had asked the farmers during meetings on Friday night and Saturday to suspend their blockade for a week while efforts were made to resolve differences.
But the farmers showed no sign of giving in. Their protests coincide with more general labour unrest and protests against a 1997 austerity budget presented by the socialists on Friday.
Much of Greece ground to a halt on Thursday during a 24-hour general strike by thousands of workers, disrupting transport, schools, hospitals and public services.
National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou said the budget would be the toughest in 15 years as Greece struggles to get its economy in line with its 14 European Union partners.
Government officials have said they were willing to seek compromise on some farmer demands but there was no question of alloting more money from the 1997 budget to agriculture.
Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas blamed the farmers' action on political manoeuvring by the Communist Party, a charge which has been hotly rejected by farm leaders.
The farmers, who began the blockade on Thursday, said they would keep up their protest until their demands were met. They have called for direct talks with Prime Minister Costas Simitis.
"This is a survival issue. We demand an immediate solution or we will stay here for as long as it takes," Yannis Pattakis, a farmers' union leader in Larissa told reporters.
It is Simitis's first major challenge since winning national elections in September to keep the socialists in power.

A farmers' revolt in March 1995 disrupted traffic through Greece or more than two weeks and savaged the economy. Tonnes of perishable goods were left to rot by the roadside and food prices soared, with Athens cut off from the agricultural north.
